rows.description: Friends and family may notice sudden withdrawal, hopeless talk, giving things away, unexplained injuries or big mood changes. These signs call for caring attention, not gossip or ignoring.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A wise friend stays calm, listens without judgment, thanks them for trusting, does not promise secrecy about safety and involves a trusted adult or helpline. Never leaves someone in immediate danger alone; emergency help is called if needed.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: gratitude, anger, calm, trust

rows.description: A parent who finds out feels fear, guilt and anger. Responding with calm concern rather than punishment or panic, and arranging professional help, protects the bond and safety.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: anger, fear, guilt, calm

rows.subtype: Hurting as a way to cope with pain [Actor]
rows.description: A person in overwhelming emotional pain may harm themselves to feel relief or numbness, then feel shame. Behind it is suffering that needs care, not punishment, and help from a professional and trusted people.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26
related mind states: shame, relief, detachment, overwhelm

rows.description: Asking gently and plainly whether someone is thinking of hurting themselves does not plant the idea and often brings relief. If the answer is yes, stay with them, remove access to danger where possible and connect to crisis services.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26
related mind states: anger, relief, hurt

rows.description: A person may feel trapped, believe they are a burden and see no way out, and may say so indirectly. Such words should always be taken seriously and met with care, company and urgent professional or emergency support.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A teenager who is struggling may fear being called weak, worry about cost or family reaction or think it is not bad enough. Many wait too long, and asking early is a sign of strength.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Adult receiving a request for help [Receiver]
rows.description: A parent or teacher whom a teenager finally approaches should stay calm, thank them for telling and act, without lecturing or dismissing. The first response often decides whether they ever ask again.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: Struggles that last weeks, affect sleep, study, work or relationships, or bring thoughts of self-harm are reasons to see a doctor, counsellor or psychologist. Trusted adults and campus services can help find the first step.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A wise person looks for licensed professionals, understands that fit matters and does not stop the process early. In a crisis, they go to emergency services or a helpline rather than waiting.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22
